horoscopes.intro: November 27 in the stars: Find out what’s in store for you today in our daily horoscopes for Friday November 27. Read the daily horoscopes for your Sun sign or rising sign (ascendant) to plan your day.

aries.text: Instead of firing off a fix-it prescription, try the Socratic method today. As the nurturing Cancer moon in your fourth house of family trines probing Mercury in your eighth house, the day after Thanksgiving is ideal for curious, philosophical conversations with any relatives still in town. Skip the Black Friday stampede and linger over leftover pie instead. Ask questions! You’ll learn so much about your loved ones when you approach them with an inquisitive mind.

taurus.text: Put on that planner’s chapeau, Taurus! Black Friday doesn’t have to be a free-for-all, especially with a harmonious trine between the Cancer moon in your local third house and savvy Mercury in your partnership zone. Team up with your favorite shopping buddy and map a strategic route through neighborhood shops. Break down your list to essentials and skip the excess bells and whistles. You can do this on a budget, so don’t feel like you have to go luxe all the way. A mix of high and low can still create a stellar, Santa-approved outcome.

gemini.text: Self-expression is the name of the game today, so let your hair down, Gemini, and give people a taste of your flair. As the Cancer moon in your second house of style trines savvy Mercury in your practical sixth house, Black Friday is prime time to score a statement piece at a markdown. Err on the side of flamboyance! Better you should be too much and overshoot the mark than miss it altogether by letting cautious conservatism stand in the way. Just set a spending cap before you hit “add to cart.”

cancer.text: If someone’s comment at yesterday’s Thanksgiving table still stings, try putting yourself in their shoes. With the moon in your sign trining articulate Mercury in your fifth house of self-expression, a person who seemed to mortally offend you may suddenly become your greatest teacher. Why? Because they illuminated an area of struggle that you can embrace and work through. Give yourself credit, Cancer: You’re stronger than you realize. Skip the mall madness and gather your support crew for a leftovers lunch.

leo.text: Today’s mantra: The more, the merrier. With the Cancer moon in your restful twelfth house trining chatty Mercury in your domestic fourth, the day after Thanksgiving is made for lounging at home with the whole gang. Let go of the need to keep anyone stuck by your side and let the crowd mingle. Skip the Black Friday lines and organize a board game tournament or a movie marathon instead. Feeling a little too much like a separate entity? A group activity helps you home in on the people you’d like to get closer to.

virgo.text: Wax on, wax off. Those micro moves you make shouldn’t be underestimated, Virgo, especially as the Cancer moon in your friendly eleventh house trines Mercury in your neighborly third. Small acts of kindness build trust with the people you want in your life for the long haul. Offer to drive a friend to the outlets or drop off leftovers at a neighbor’s door. Show off your dependable nature, because important people are taking note!

libra.text: Be the ray of sunshine, Libra, the one who sees possibilities where others only see dead-ends. With the Cancer moon in your tenth house of leadership trining Mercury in your second house of values, people may look to you to lift the mood, whether you’re clocking in today or braving the Black Friday crowds. Just don’t fall into the Pollyanna role, or you could accidentally minimize other people’s frustrations. Let them air their grievances. Then, from a place of compassion, you can turn them toward the brighter side.

scorpio.text: Your psychic powers are in fine form today, Scorpio, as the Cancer moon trines Mercury in your sign. Don’t let people talk you out of your intuitive hits. You’re not just being paranoid (although there’s a chance you could be overreacting). Follow the breadcrumb trail and research the facts. That goes double for Black Friday “deals” that look too good to be true, so compare prices before you click. Listening to your gut and then checking the details could change a loved one’s day—or at least save you a bundle.

sagittarius.text: No one person can be your “everything,” Sagittarius. Even if you’re feeling possessive as the Cancer moon in your intimate eighth house trines Mercury in your twelfth house, take the path of least resistance and unclasp the red velvet rope. Don’t resist if your post-Thanksgiving hangout expands from two to six. Maybe you’ve forgotten how much you thrive in a “more the merrier” environment. A friend’s wild-card plus-one could be the very person you’ve been wanting to meet!

capricorn.text: No, Capricorn, money can’t buy you love, but it sure can make life a whole lot more comfortable. Today’s trine between the Cancer moon in your partnership zone and Mercury in your eleventh house of technology makes Black Friday a smart time to score a shareable gadget you and your sweetie or a close friend both need. Prioritize! It’s easy to get swept up in the minutiae of doorbuster deals, so map out a plan instead of shooting from the hip.

aquarius.text: Take a leap of faith, Aquarius! A propitious trine between the Cancer moon in your sixth house of daily routines and Mercury in your tenth house of career gives you good reason to try something new. While everyone else is out shopping, use the down day to polish your portfolio or pitch a passion project. You might hit a few bumps while you figure out where your new edges lie. Still, you’ll attract some major attention, so harness this energy and promote your talents!

pisces.text: No superficial small talk for you today, Pisces. (Or maybe ever?!) As the Cancer moon in your fifth house of romance trines Mercury in your philosophical ninth house, you’re craving deep and meaningful conversation. Skip the Black Friday frenzy and linger over happy-hour cocktails with your BFF, or invite a fellow Friday-night yogi to a vegan dinner after class. Don’t overlook the quiet ones in your circle. Ask how they’re feeling and let them weigh in on a matter that’s been on your mind. Their empathy and depth will be a match for your own.

items.title: Neurotransmitter pathway-specific polygenic risk for psychiatric disorders and brain morphology in adolescents
items.originalTitle: Neurotransmitter pathway-specific polygenic risk for psychiatric disorders and brain morphology in adolescents
items.summary: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Schizophrenia (SCZ), and Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) are highly heritable and have been linked to brain morphology.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Schizophrenia (SCZ), and Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) are highly heritable and have been linked to brain morphology. We investigated how genetic variation in neurotransmitter systems is associated with brain morphology using pathway-specific polygenic risk scores (PGS) in adolescence. We studied 8591 participants of European ancestry (ages 9-14 years; 13,551 brain images) from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development and the Generation R Study. Genome-wide PGS for ADHD, SCZ, and MDD were computed alongside pathway-specific PGSs for the glutamate, GABA, dopamine, and serotonin pathways. Vertex-wise mega-analyses of cortical surface area and thickness using linear mixed-effects random-intercept models were conducted. Genome-wide and pathway-specific PGSs for ADHD were associated with smaller cortical surface area, with spatially extensive genome-wide clusters (82,508 mm²) and more localized pathway-specific clusters (up to 10,237 mm²). For SCZ, pathway-specific PGSs were associated with significant surface-area clusters totaling 4302 mm², compared with 1129 mm² for the genome-wide PGS. The serotonin PGS for SCZ was linked to a smaller lingual gyrus (1041 mm²), while the GABA PGS was associated with a larger surface area in temporal and cingulate regions (2004 mm²). A higher genome-wide PGS for MDD was related to a smaller surface area (4936 mm²) in frontotemporal regions. Pathway-specific PGSs for MDD were associated with a smaller orbitofrontal (glutamate) and precuneus (GABA) surface area, with cluster sizes between 197-297 mm². Associations with cortical thickness were limited. These results demonstrate that partitioning genetic risk for ADHD, SCZ, and MDD into neurotransmitter-specific pathways reveals distinct cortical surface area signatures in adolescence.

items.title: Empirical evidence for eight ways that AI is impacting people
items.originalTitle: Empirical evidence for eight ways that AI is impacting people
items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are now used by one billion people worldwide. What is their impact on human users?
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are now used by one billion people worldwide. What is their impact on human users? Popular narratives of concern argue that AI may be undermining our cognitive abilities, polluting our information ecosystem, corroding human relationships, damaging our mental health and rendering us vulnerable to persuasion, manipulation, emotional dependence and social engineering. Does the empirical evidence support these claims? Emerging research has begun to study the impact that AI has on people, via model evaluations, user studies, analysis of consumer chatlogs and agent-based simulations. Here we review this evidence, finding limited evidence for the strongest narratives of concern. However, research is still nascent and many uncertainties remain to be resolved in future work.

items.title: Genetic mechanisms underlying the associations between brain structure and mental health
items.originalTitle: Genetic mechanisms underlying the associations between brain structure and mental health
items.summary: Brain-wide association studies have linked brain structure to complex mental health phenotypes, yet the genetic underpinnings of these effects remain largely unclear.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: Brain-wide association studies have linked brain structure to complex mental health phenotypes, yet the genetic underpinnings of these effects remain largely unclear. Here, we leverage multimodal neuroimaging, behavioral and genetic data from the UK Biobank to develop an integrative framework combining brain-wide association studies and GWAS to elucidate how genetic variants affect the relationship between brain structure and mental health. Our multivariate brain-wide association study identifies two reproducible brain structural modes: a cerebellar-dominant mode and a cortical-dominant mode that explain individual differences in mental health measures. Using GWAS, we subsequently identify 30 and 15 independent significant variants respectively for each mode, indicating distinct genetic architectures with no signal overlap. Post-GWAS analyses indicate distinct biological pathways: the cerebellar-dominant mode is enriched for genes involved in chromatin organization and epigenetic regulation, while the cortical-dominant mode is linked to neurotransmitter metabolism. Moreover, we identify shared genetic influences between the brain modes and both mental health and cognitive traits, as well as causal effects of the brain modes on these outcomes. We validate the framework in the independent HCP cohort, supporting the cross-cohort generalizability of the identified brain-behavior and genetic associations.

items.title: The nucleus accumbens: an emerging modulator in anxiety disorders
items.originalTitle: The nucleus accumbens: an emerging modulator in anxiety disorders
items.summary: Anxiety disorders are common mental health conditions that significantly reduce quality of life and strain healthcare systems worldwide.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: Anxiety disorders are common mental health conditions that significantly reduce quality of life and strain healthcare systems worldwide. Although traditionally known for its central role in reward processing, the nucleus accumbens (NAc) is increasingly recognized as a critical integrative node linking stress responses and motivational networks to modulate anxiety-related behaviors. This review summarizes recent findings on the NAc's role in anxiety regulation, focusing on neurotransmitter systems, including opioid receptors, oxytocin, and the endocannabinoid system, as well as glial mechanisms involving microglia and astrocytes. Additionally, we discuss the neural circuits that connect the NAc to regions such as the ventral tegmental area, the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, and the medial prefrontal cortex, providing circuit-level insights. Emerging treatments, including pharmacological approaches such as ketamine and non-pharmacological strategies like exercise and deep brain stimulation, highlight the potential to target the NAc in anxiety disorders. Emphasizing the integration of molecular, cellular, and circuit perspectives, this review underscores the NAc's central role in anxiety regulation and calls for further research to develop more precise treatments.

items.title: This dietary supplement may have an unexpected benefit for the brain
items.originalTitle: This dietary supplement may have an unexpected benefit for the brain
items.summary: A naturally derived dietary supplement called urolithin A may help the brain get more oxygen and nutrients when it needs them most.
items.caution: Strongest kind of evidence — still check who took part.
items.abstract: A naturally derived dietary supplement called urolithin A may help the brain get more oxygen and nutrients when it needs them most. In a randomized clinical trial involving 50 middle-aged adults with obesity, researchers found that taking the supplement daily for four weeks increased blood flow to the brain during a challenging memory task, particularly in a region involved in working memory.

items.title: Frontal ripples cooperate with mixed-selectivity neurons for compositional sequence control
items.originalTitle: Frontal ripples cooperate with mixed-selectivity neurons for compositional sequence control
items.summary: In mammals, bursts of high-frequency local field potential oscillations, or "ripples," often accompany sequential spatiotemporal associations. However, whether and how ripples support the control of sequences remains largely unexplored.
items.caution: In animals or cells — may not carry over to people.
items.abstract: In mammals, bursts of high-frequency local field potential oscillations, or "ripples," often accompany sequential spatiotemporal associations. However, whether and how ripples support the control of sequences remains largely unexplored. We trained two macaque monkeys to perform a visuospatial sequence working memory task that required flexible assembly and manipulation of sequence constituents. We found that frontal ripples preferentially cooccurred with mixed-selectivity neurons that encoded multiple sequence items and that ripple rates predicted the neurons' contributions to sequence representations. Crucially, co-ripples and phasic synchronization with local spiking activity delineated a potential time window for coordinating or binding sequence constituent information. Furthermore, this binding process could be generalized to longer sequences and even sequence reconstruction. Thus, coupling of frontal cortical ripples with mixed-selectivity neurons underlies sequence formation and reorganization in working memory.

items.title: A gut-brain sensory-motor circuit regulates sugar ingestion in Drosophila
items.originalTitle: A gut-brain sensory-motor circuit regulates sugar ingestion in Drosophila
items.summary: Bidirectional communication between the brain and digestive tract is critical for optimizing nutrient preference and food intake, yet the neural mechanisms that couple gut nutrient sensing with ingestive motor control remain poorly understood.
items.caution: In animals or cells — may not carry over to people.
items.abstract: Bidirectional communication between the brain and digestive tract is critical for optimizing nutrient preference and food intake, yet the neural mechanisms that couple gut nutrient sensing with ingestive motor control remain poorly understood. Here we identify a gut-brain sensory-motor circuit that regulates sugar ingestion in flies. We show that the brain neurons that regulate food ingestion, IN1s1, receive excitatory input from enteric sensory neurons that penetrate the foregut epithelium and detect sugars in the gut lumen during ingestion. Functional imaging and connectome analyses reveal that IN1s integrate excitatory input from multiple sugar-sensing neurons, including enteric sensory neurons, and provide inhibitory output to enteric motor neurons that control the muscles at the entry of the crop-a stomach-like organ. During ingestion, IN1 activation suppresses these enteric motor neurons, relaxes the crop duct and promotes rapid transfer of food into the crop, thereby enabling sustained food intake. Together, our findings describe a gut-brain circuit that controls the motor activity of digestive tract muscles during feeding and suggest a circuit mechanism by which nutrient signals from the gut contribute to the dynamic regulation of food intake across metabolic states.

items.title: Implementing Digital Mental Health Interventions for Children and Young People in Emergency Care Settings: Systematic Review
items.originalTitle: Implementing Digital Mental Health Interventions for Children and Young People in Emergency Care Settings: Systematic Review
items.summary: Emergency departments play a central role in crisis management for children and young people's (CYP) mental health. These settings face significant challenges in delivering effective support, such as shortages of mental health specialists, long waiting times, and overcrowding.
items.caution: Strongest kind of evidence — still check who took part.
items.abstract:
Background: Emergency departments play a central role in crisis management for children and young people's (CYP) mental health. These settings face significant challenges in delivering effective support, such as shortages of mental health specialists, long waiting times, and overcrowding. Digital mental health interventions (DMHIs) may have the potential to expand access to care, bridge service gaps, and alleviate pressure on emergency settings for CYP experiencing mental health crises.

Objective: This review systematically reviews the current evidence for the acceptability, appropriateness, feasibility, and cost-effectiveness of DMHIs for CYP in emergency care settings.

Methods: We conducted database searches using APA PsycInfo, Embase, MEDLINE, and Web of Science from January 2015 to September 2025. We included quantitative, qualitative, and mixed methods studies that related to the acceptability, appropriateness, feasibility, and cost-effectiveness of DMHIs in acute settings. Acceptability, appropriateness, and feasibility were added as post hoc outcomes for this secondary review after implementation-related evidence was identified in the original search. DMHIs included telepsychiatry, phone calls, SMS text messaging, and computerized interventions. In addition to studies reporting data from CYP under the age of 25 years, we included those evaluating data from caregivers and care providers. All selected studies were assessed for quality using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool.

Results: Overall, 6778 articles were retrieved from the database searches, of which 13 articles met the inclusion criteria. In total, data from 1495 patients, of whom 1048 received a DMHI, 413 caregivers, and 250 care providers were included across studies, excluding 1 study that did not report the sample size for care providers. Mental health presentations included depressive symptoms, violent behaviors, suicidal ideation and attempts, intoxication, and multiple mental health conditions. DMHIs were broadly acceptable, particularly for interventions such as telepsychiatry and structured follow-up phone calls. Feasibility, appropriateness, and cost-effectiveness outcomes were more varied. These were affected by the specific intervention design, emergency care context, and user characteristics. items.title: Hippocampal representations differentiate reactive and anticipatory responses during foraging under threat
items.originalTitle: Hippocampal representations differentiate reactive and anticipatory responses during foraging under threat
items.summary: Adaptive behavior under threat requires balancing reward pursuit against the risk of harm. During approach-avoidance conflict, animals often pause at decision points, but whether these pauses reflect a unified process or distinct decision states remains unclear.
items.caution: In animals or cells — may not carry over to people.
items.abstract: Adaptive behavior under threat requires balancing reward pursuit against the risk of harm. During approach-avoidance conflict, animals often pause at decision points, but whether these pauses reflect a unified process or distinct decision states remains unclear. Here, we replicate and extend findings from Calvin et al., 2025, by analyzing hippocampal activity in rats performing a pseudo-predator foraging task across two cohorts. We compared mid-track aborts (MTAs), mid-track continues (MTCs), and retreats. Behaviorally, MTAs and MTCs emerged from a shared pause state but diverged in outcome, whereas retreats reflected rapid escape following attack. Despite similar endpoints, retreats and MTAs differed in movement dynamics and neural activity. During retreats, hippocampal representations remained biased toward the attack location. In contrast, representations during MTAs shifted toward safe locations. During pauses, representations differed according to subsequent behavior: pauses preceding MTAs showed greater decoded probability near the attack region, whereas pauses preceding MTCs showed greater decoded probability to goal locations. These differences were present during the outbound approach, suggesting decision-related processes emerged early on in the journey. Together, these findings dissociate hippocampal representations associated with reactive escape from those underlying anticipatory, anxiety-like decision-making, suggesting that the hippocampus dynamically tracks behaviorally relevant features to guide decisions under threat.

items.title: Biotin intake and mental health: findings from a large population-based cohort and biological insights from hippocampal and gut-brain pathways
items.originalTitle: Biotin intake and mental health: findings from a large population-based cohort and biological insights from hippocampal and gut-brain pathways
items.summary: The relationship between biotin and mental health remains largely unexplored.
items.caution: In animals or cells — may not carry over to people.
items.abstract: The relationship between biotin and mental health remains largely unexplored. Leveraging data from the UK Biobank prospective cohort, we found that dietary biotin intake in the second quartile was associated with a 15% lower risk of major depressive disorder, while intake in the third quartile was associated with a 14% lower risk of anxiety disorder, compared with the lowest quartile. Furthermore, restricted cubic spline (RCS) analyses revealed nonlinear associations between dietary biotin intake and both outcomes, with the lowest risks of incidence observed at biotin intake levels of approximately 40-50 μg. Neuroimaging analyses further revealed positive associations between dietary biotin intake and fractional anisotropy in the cingulum-hippocampus tract, suggesting a potential link between biotin intake and white matter microstructure in a pathway involved in emotional regulation. We then examined the effects of a 9-week biotin intervention in mice and observed changes consistent with two potential pathways: a hippocampus-related pathway involving enhanced protein biotinylation, reduced neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) expression, and increased brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) expression, and a gut-brain axis pathway characterized by greater microbial diversity and an increased relative abundance of Akkermansia muciniphila, which was positively associated with brain 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) levels. These findings provide complementary biological evidence that may help explain the observed association between dietary biotin intake and mental health.
